title: Learning to measure the air.
summary: A student-built wind tunnel, dry-ice flow visualization, and a measurement stand taking shape.
text: How can a small wind tunnel produce measurements we can trust? Arduino BME280 HX711 / load cells 3D printing Python A working fieldbook of a wind tunnel and its instruments. Rithwik leads the build and research; Rithika documents the work, proposed the dry-ice approach, helped review code, and explores CubeSat possibilities. The latest account is a **user-reported update received 13 October 2026**, not an independently verified performance test. The project connects an observable flow with the harder question of measuring forces reliably. The tunnel is a platform for learning aerodynamics, instrumentation, fabrication, and analysis together. The stand needs to support airfoils and model aircraft while enabling lift and drag measurement. Sensor calibration, mounting geometry, repeatable conditions, and an uncertainty estimate remain necessary. Numerical design requirements and acceptance thresholds have not yet been supplied. The reported tunnel has a plexiglass test body with printed supports and inlet/outlet components. **Dry ice is placed in water in front of the inlet. Air is blown into that setup, and an outlet fan draws it through the tunnel.** The new stand uses differential pressure, load cells for lift and drag, and a BME280 for environmental conditions. The exact pressure-sensor model remains unconfirmed. Repeated smoke-system setbacks prompted a change in visualization method. Rithika proposed dry ice. A visible flow pattern helps observe movement, but it does not by itself establish flow uniformity, airspeed, or measurement accuracy. The stand must also balance mechanical support with interference in the flow; that trade-off is still open. The earlier Arduino code contains a modeled differential-pressure channel with simulated noise and conditioning. It is an inspectable software artifact. A verified pressure-to-speed calculation requires an appropriate pressure measurement, air-density assumptions, and a calibrated sensor. No validated CFD, airspeed, lift, or drag result is currently available. The October 3 update reports a built two-fan tunnel, printed inlet/outlet, plexiglass body, and printed supports. The October 13 update adds a measurement stand still being developed. A **3D model to accommodate airfoils and model aircraft is planned**. Updated stand CAD and source will be added to GitHub later; existing files remain the linked evidence. **Proposed next procedure:** document the final stand and wiring; calibrate each force channel against a known reference; establish zero and repeatability; record ambient conditions; then define controlled comparison runs. This is a planning outline, not a performed experiment or an approved calibration protocol. Rithwik reports that the dry-ice setup produces a smooth visible flow into the inlet. This is a qualitative build observation. **No measured aerodynamic results or completed calibration records have been supplied.** The available CSV rows below are software sample input only. The original smoke approach required repeated changes to materials, filaments, air pumps, and the setup. The shift to dry ice in water is the documented response. A dated run-by-run failure log and photographs are still needed to make those iterations reproducible. Repository code, 3MF archives, and embedded previews can be inspected. Physical accuracy is not established by those files. Outstanding evidence includes updated wiring and stand CAD, calibration records, repeat trials, reference measurements, and an uncertainty budget. The latest stand is unfinished. No completed airfoil/aircraft mounting model, exact new pressure-sensor part number, flow-uniformity map, or force dataset has been supplied. The GitHub record predates the latest reported hardware configuration. The documented iteration separates making a phenomenon visible from measuring it. The change in visualization method solved a reported practical obstacle; reliable force measurement remains the next learning task. More detailed personal reflections can be added as they are recorded. Finish the stand model, document how airfoils and model aircraft attach, complete calibration, publish the updated source and original photographs, and collect repeatable measurements with their limitations.

title: From a signal to a useful record.
summary: CSV plotting and an offset-correction prototype for inspecting environmental data.
text: How do we make collected sensor data inspectable without confusing correction with calibration? Python CSV Flask Arduino The Python grapher reads environmental channels and creates plots. A separate Flask prototype explores offset correction, summary statistics, and CSV export. These tools support the wind-tunnel project. A record is easier to question when its raw values, units, and transformations stay visible. Plotting is part of inspection; it is not proof of sensor accuracy. Keep raw and transformed data distinct. Preserve timestamps and units. The Flask prototype requires its own runtime and is linked as source; it does not run on GitHub Pages. The earlier firmware schedules CSV records every two seconds. That is a configured interval, not a benchmark. A separate correction tool makes offsets inspectable but risks implying accuracy if calibration records are absent. The earlier modeled pressure channel includes noise and conditioning. Default offsets in the correction prototype are not treated as measured calibration coefficients. Source files for the logger, grapher, and correction tool exist in the linked repository. The current website provides a lightweight viewer for the exact three-row sample fixture. The sample values demonstrate software input. They are not measured wind-tunnel results and cannot support claims about lift, drag, or flow uniformity. No dated software failure log is present in the reviewed record. The available limitation is the absence of independent calibration evidence for default offsets. The website checks that chart coordinates and table values reproduce the supplied fixture. This verifies display behavior only; it does not validate the original instruments or research software. title: A clearer flow. A new measurement stand.
summary: Dry ice in water makes the inlet flow visible. The next challenge is a stand that can hold airfoils and model aircraft.
text:
Instrumentation Fabrication Flow visualization ## Research objective

Develop the wind-tunnel measurement stand so it can accommodate airfoils and model aircraft while supporting lift, drag, pressure, and environmental measurements.

## The current setup

Dry ice sits in water in front of the inlet. Air is blown into that setup so the visible flow enters the tunnel; a fan on the opposite side draws air out. The owner reports that the visualization flows smoothly. That description is a qualitative observation, not a measured flow-uniformity result.

## Materials and instruments

| Element | Current account |
| --- | --- |
| Visualization | Dry ice in water in front of the inlet |
| Air movement | Air blown into the inlet setup; outlet fan draws air out |
| Pressure | Differential-pressure sensor; exact model not supplied |
| Forces | Load cells intended for lift and drag measurements |
| Environment | BME280 for environmental conditions |
| Mounting | New stand under development; 3D model planned |

The earlier record identifies HX711 interfaces for the load cells. New wiring and source have not yet been posted, so the linked Arduino program remains an earlier implementation.

## Design question

How should the stand support different test objects while keeping the load paths clear and the sensor readings interpretable?

## Method and observations

This entry records the owner's description of the present build. It is not a test procedure. No loads, airspeeds, sensor readings, acceptance thresholds, or repeated trials were supplied with the update.

## What is still open

The stand is unfinished. The next step is a 3D model that can accommodate airfoils and model aircraft. Calibration was unfinished in the previous record; no completion update has been provided.

## What changed

The visualization approach has moved away from the troublesome smoke system. The present focus is shifting toward the measurement stand. The archived files remain useful evidence, but should not be mistaken for the latest stand configuration.

## Next steps

- Finish and document the stand model.
- Record mounting geometry, sensor connections, and channel definitions.
- Complete calibration and publish the procedure and raw records.
- Add the updated files and photographs to GitHub.

## Revision record

**13 October 2026:** Created from the owner's update. The owner clarified that “cold dryers” meant dry ice placed in water. No new measurements were added.

title: Before the plot, calibrate the measurement.
summary: What remains to be established before a corrected sensor value can support an aerodynamic claim.
text:
Instrumentation Uncertainty ## Research objective

Separate a useful plot from a defensible measurement. The current stand needs a way to connect sensor readings to known reference values before those readings can support force measurements.

## Background research

The earlier correction prototype contains default offsets. Subtracting an offset changes a number; a reference comparison is needed to justify the correction. The Arduino source also includes a modeled pressure channel with simulated noise and conditioning.

## Proposed method

This is a planning note. Document a reference, collect repeat readings at known conditions, record zero behavior and drift, then evaluate how the response changes across the intended range. Keep the raw observations alongside any fit or correction.

## Technical context

For a flow with density $\rho$ and speed $V$, dynamic pressure is:

$$q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2$$

If a suitable measurement establishes dynamic pressure, the corresponding relation is:

$$V = \sqrt{\frac{2q}{\rho}}$$

These are general relations, not results from this tunnel. Applying them requires an appropriate pressure arrangement, density assumptions, and a calibrated measurement. A generic differential-pressure sensor reading is not automatically dynamic pressure.

## Data and observations

No reference-calibration dataset has been supplied. No coefficients, fit quality, or uncertainty values are asserted here.

## What could go wrong

Mounting interference, zero drift, cross-axis sensitivity, incorrect units, or treating a modeled input as a physical reading could all undermine an interpretation. These are proposed checks, not observed failures of this stand.

## What this note establishes

The question is not whether software can draw a smooth line. It is whether the value on that line can be traced to a documented measurement process.

## Next steps

Choose and document reference checks for each channel once the stand geometry is settled. Record assumptions and uncertainty before reporting aerodynamic conclusions.

title: Three rows, and what they can actually tell us.
summary: Inspecting the exact sample input used by the environmental-data grapher, without treating it as an experiment.
text:
Python Data analysis ## Research objective

Inspect the input format used by the Python environmental-data grapher. The existing sample contains three rows dated 4 March 2026. They are example input, not wind-tunnel results.

## Software

The repository includes a Python grapher and a separate Flask correction prototype. This fieldbook's viewer displays the supplied rows without smoothing or extrapolation.

## Method

Read each channel with its unit. Preserve the source values. Plot elapsed minutes on the horizontal axis and one selected channel on the vertical axis. Make the underlying table available beside the chart.

```python
# Illustrative inspection of the repository sample format.
# This snippet is educational, not a quoted project implementation.
import csv

with open("sample.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as source:
    for row in csv.DictReader(source):
        print(row)
```

## Data and analysis

The sample temperature values are 23.4, 23.5, and 23.6 °C. Humidity is 41.2, 41.0, and 40.9 %. Pressure is 1008.6, 1008.7, and 1008.8 hPa. These values demonstrate the file format. Three sample rows cannot establish an environmental trend or aerodynamic result.

## What could go wrong

A plot can look authoritative even when its input is only a fixture. The viewer therefore carries a persistent “Sample input only” label and a direct source link. Changing the chart type does not change the evidence status.

## What this note establishes

Data display and measurement validation are separate tasks. A faithful visualization preserves provenance, units, and limitations along with the numbers.

## Next steps

When actual experiments produce datasets, add the acquisition method, instrument configuration, calibration record, repeat runs, and uncertainty information to the same content structure.

title: Reading a honeycomb, one layer at a time.
summary: A print archive contains more than a thumbnail. The extrusion moves reveal the honeycomb layer itself.
text:
Fabrication Geometry ## Research objective

Expose the geometry recorded in the current honeycomb print archive without pretending it is a flow simulation.

## Source material

The repository contains four sliced 3MF archives: two honeycomb files, a holder, and support corners. The source record does not establish which archived versions were fabricated in the later build.

## Method

The existing visualization was reconstructed from `Metadata/plate_1.gcode` in `honeyComb_Current.gcode.3mf`. It uses 3,724 positive-extrusion XY line segments in the slice whose `Z_HEIGHT` is 10 mm. Travel-only moves are omitted.

Coordinates were mapped uniformly into a 600 × 540 illustration and rounded to 0.1 display units. The preview in the archive showed a solid slab; the layer trace reveals the honeycomb infill.

## Observations

The image is a digital fabrication artifact. Its paths are evidence of instructions in the archive, not a photograph of a printed part, a dimensioned manufacturing drawing, or a measured flow field.

## Analysis and limitations

Filenames alone do not explain why a design changed. A layer trace also cannot establish how accurately a printer reproduced the part or how the finished honeycomb affects the flow.

## What this note establishes

A source artifact becomes more useful when a reader can inspect both the rendering and the original file. The caption is part of the evidence: it defines what the image can and cannot show.

## Next steps

Link fabricated parts to exact archive versions. Add original photographs, dimensions, and test records when available.
